title: Binary Heap
html:
A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in a plain array in which every parent is smaller (min-heap) or larger (max-heap) than its children. It gives the minimum in O(1) and insert / extract-min in O(log n) with no pointers at all — it is the structure behind every priority queue and heap sort.

Binary heap — an array a viewed as a complete binary tree — a[0] is the root, the children of a[i] are a[2i + 1] and a[2i + 2] — that satisfies the heap property: in a min-heap every node is ≤ its children (so the minimum is at the root); in a max-heap every node is ≥ its children (the maximum is at the root).

Used in heap sort and to implement a priority queue — the data structure of always give me the most urgent item: Dijkstra's and Prim's algorithms, Huffman coding, event schedulers, the k largest and running median problems.

A complete binary tree stored as an array

The array trick only works because a heap is a complete binary tree: every level is full except possibly the last, and that one is filled strictly from left to right. Reading such a tree level by level leaves no gaps, so position in the array ↔ position in the tree, and the parent/child relations become arithmetic.

Relation0-based array (used here)1-based array (the notes' first version)
Roota[0]a[1]
Parent of i(i − 1) / 2 (integer division)i / 2
Left child of i2i + 12i
Right child of i2i + 22i + 1
Leavesindices n/2 … n − 1indices n/2 + 1 … n
Last internal noden/2 − 1n/2

Because a complete tree of n nodes has height ⌊log₂ n⌋, every root-to-leaf walk — which is what insert and extract do — takes O(log n) steps. And because there are no pointers, a heap of n ints is exactly n ints of memory, laid out contiguously and cache-friendly.

Key point

A heap is not a search structure. The heap property says nothing about the relation between the two subtrees of a node — 15 is left of 5 in the example above — so finding an arbitrary value is O(n). If you need search and min/max, use a balanced BST.

Min-heap and max-heap

Min-heapMax-heap
Heap propertyevery node ≤ its children (and so ≤ all its descendants)every node ≥ its children
Root holdsthe minimumthe maximum
Priority queuethe item with the lowest value has the highest prioritythe item with the highest value has the highest priority
Default inPython heapq, Java PriorityQueueC++ std::priority_queue

Everything below is written for a min-heap; a max-heap is the same code with every comparison flipped — or, cheaper, a min-heap of the negated values.

Which of these are min-heaps? (from the notes)

Operations and their cost

OperationHowTimeWhy
getMin() / peek()Return a[0]O(1)The root is always the minimum
insert(x)Append at the end, then sift up while smaller than the parentO(log n)Climbs at most the height of the tree
extractMin()Move the last element to the root, then sift down (heapify)O(log n)Descends at most the height
decreaseKey(i, x)Lower a[i] to x, then sift upO(log n)Only the path to the root can be violated
delete(i)decreaseKey(i, −∞) then extractMin()O(log n)Two logarithmic steps
buildHeap(arr)Heapify every internal node from the last one up to the rootO(n)Most nodes are near the bottom and move only a few levels
search for a valueScan the arrayO(n)No ordering between siblings

Insert (sift up)

Example

Input: insert 3, 2, 15, 5, 4, 45 into an empty min-heap
Output: array 2 3 15 5 4 45 — min 2

Idea

Put the new element in the first free slot (a[n]) — that keeps the tree complete. The only thing that can now be wrong is that the new element is smaller than its parent, so swap it upward until its parent is smaller or it reaches the root. Each swap fixes the pair without disturbing anything else, and the walk is at most h = ⌊log₂ n⌋ steps.

Time O(log n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

In JavaScript (i - 1) / 2 is a float — Math.floor is required. In Python use //. Forgetting this gives fractional indices and a heap that silently never sifts.

Extract min (sift down / heapify)

Example

Input: the heap 2 3 15 5 4 45
Output: returns 2; heap becomes 3 4 15 5 45
Input: extract again
Output: returns 3; heap becomes 4 5 15 45

Idea

The minimum is the root, but removing the root leaves a hole at the top and a complete tree can only lose its last slot. So: save a[0], move the last element into the root, shrink the array by one. The only violation now is at the root, which may be larger than a child — sift it down: swap it with the smaller of its two children (so the new parent is ≤ both) and repeat from there until it is ≤ both children or becomes a leaf. This repair step is minHeapify(i) — it assumes both subtrees of i are valid heaps and fixes node i.

Time O(log n)Space O(log n) for the recursive heapify — O(1) if written as a loop
Pitfall

minHeapify must swap with the smaller child, not just any smaller child. Swapping with the larger one puts it above its sibling and breaks the heap property. Also check l < n / r < n before reading — the notes' first version read a[rightChild] past the end when a node had only a left child.

Decrease key and delete

Example

Input: the heap 2 3 15 5 4 45; decreaseKey(index 2, 1)
Output: 15 becomes 1 and rises to the root: 1 3 2 5 4 45
Input: then delete(index 1)
Output: the value 3 is removed: 1 4 2 5 45

Idea

Decrease key lowers one value. A smaller value can only violate the heap property with its parent, so the fix is the same sift-up as insert. Delete at index i needs no new mechanism: decrease the key to −∞ so it rises to the root, then extractMin() throws it away. Both are O(log n). (Increase key would be the mirror: set the value, then minHeapify(i).)

Time O(log n) eachSpace O(1)
Key point

decreaseKey is what Dijkstra's algorithm needs when a shorter path to a vertex is found. It requires knowing the index of the element, which the array can only provide with an extra value → index map; the library priority queues below do not offer it, so Dijkstra implementations usually push a fresh entry instead (lazy deletion).

Pitfall

The notes' second implementation had two typos that make it silently wrong: lchild returned 2 * 1 + 1 (always 3) instead of 2 * i + 1, and decreasekey compared arr[self.parent(i) > arr[i]] — indexing with a boolean — instead of arr[self.parent(i)] > arr[i]. Running the code with a known heap and checking the array after every operation, as above, catches both.

Build heap in O(n)

Example

Input: arr = 40 10 30 50 20 15
Output: min-heap 10 20 15 50 40 30

Idea

Inserting n elements one by one costs O(n log n). Building bottom-up is faster: the leaves (indices n/2 … n − 1) are already one-node heaps, so call minHeapify(i) for i = n/2 − 1 down to 0. Each call assumes both subtrees are heaps — true, because every index below i was fixed first — and repairs node i by sifting it down.

Why O(n) and not O(n log n). A node at height h (leaves at height 0) sifts down at most h steps, and there are at most n / 2^(h+1) nodes at that height. Total work is Σ h · n / 2^(h+1) = n · Σ h / 2^(h+1) ≤ n · 1 = O(n) — half the nodes are leaves and cost nothing, a quarter move at most one level, and so on. The O(n log n) bound counts log n for every node, which is far too pessimistic.

Time O(n) to build; O(n log n) to extract everythingSpace O(1) extra (in place)
Key point

Build heap, then extract everything is already a sorting algorithm — the extraction order is ascending. Heap sort below does the same thing in place, without a second array, by using a max-heap.

Heap sort

Example

Input: arr = 40 10 30 50 20 15
Output: 10 15 20 30 40 50

Idea

Build a max-heap in place (O(n)). The maximum is now at a[0]; swap it with the last element so it sits in its final sorted position, shrink the heap by one and maxHeapify(0) to restore the heap on the remaining prefix. Repeat n − 1 times: each round places one more element at the end, so the sorted suffix grows while the heap prefix shrinks — all inside the same array.

1
Build max-heap
for i = n/2 − 1 … 0: maxHeapify(a, n, i) — the largest element is at a[0].
2
Repeat for end = n − 1 … 1
Swap a[0] and a[end] (the max is now in place), then maxHeapify(a, end, 0) on the prefix of length end.
3
Done
The prefix shrinks to one element; the array is sorted ascending.
Time O(n log n) always — no bad inputSpace O(1) extra (in place; O(log n) stack if heapify is recursive)
Heap sortMerge sortQuick sort
Worst caseO(n log n)O(n log n)O(n²)
Extra spaceO(1)O(n)O(log n) stack
StableNoYesNo
In practiceSlower (poor cache locality: jumps across the array)Fast, used for linked lists and external sortingFastest on arrays; libraries use introsort = quick sort that falls back to heap sort

Built-in priority queues

You will rarely write a heap by hand outside an interview. Every language but JavaScript ships one; the API is always push, pop the best, peek.

LanguagePriority queueDefault orderpush / pop / peekMax-heap instead
Pythonheapq — functions on a plain listmin-heapheappush(h, x) / heappop(h) / h[0]push -x, or (−priority, item) tuples
C++std::priority_queue<T>max-heappush(x) / pop() (returns nothing) / top()it is max by default; min: priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>>
Javajava.util.PriorityQueue<T>min-heapoffer(x) / poll() / peek()new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder())
JavaScript— none built inwrite a MinHeap class (below) or use a library
Example

Input: start from 5 20 1 30 4; push 3; pop everything
Output: min 1; popped order 1 3 4 5 20 30

Time O(log n) push / pop, O(1) peekSpace O(n)

heapq also has a few conveniences worth knowing — nlargest, nsmallest and heapreplace (pop then push in a single sift, faster than the two calls). The list is the heap, so you can print it and see the array layout from the diagrams:

Pitfall

A heap is not sorted — only h[0] is guaranteed to be the minimum. Iterating over heapq's list, PriorityQueue's iterator or printing the array gives level order, not ascending order. To get sorted output, pop repeatedly.

Key point

For a max-heap in Python push the negated values (heappush(h, -x), read -h[0]); for tuples (priority, item) the heap orders by priority first — make sure items are comparable or add a tie-breaking counter. In Java pass Collections.reverseOrder() or a Comparator; in C++ the default priority_queue<int> already is a max-heap.

Where heaps are used

Priority queue

Task scheduling, event simulation, bandwidth management — serve the most urgent item first, O(log n) per operation.

Heap sort

O(n log n) worst case with O(1) extra space; the fallback inside introsort.

Graph algorithms

Dijkstra's shortest paths and Prim's minimum spanning tree pop the closest vertex from a min-heap.

k largest / smallest

Keep a min-heap of size k; push each element and pop when the size exceeds k — O(n log k) instead of sorting everything.

Median of a stream

A max-heap of the lower half and a min-heap of the upper half; the median is at the roots.

Merge k sorted lists

Push the head of each list; pop the smallest and push its successor — O(N log k). Huffman coding uses the same pattern.

Interview Q&A

Why can a heap be stored in an array but a BST cannot?

A heap is a complete binary tree, so reading it level by level leaves no gaps and parent/child positions are pure arithmetic ((i−1)/2, 2i+1, 2i+2). A BST can have any shape; storing it the same way would need an array of size 2^h with mostly empty slots.

Why is building a heap O(n) when a single insert is O(log n)?

Bottom-up build calls heapify on the internal nodes from the bottom, and a node at height h sifts down at most h levels. Half of the nodes are leaves (cost 0), a quarter are at height 1, an eighth at height 2 … so the total is n · Σ h / 2^(h+1), a series that converges to n. Inserting one by one instead sifts up, and most elements are deep, so that is Θ(n log n).

Heap or balanced BST for a priority queue?

A heap: O(1) peek, O(log n) push/pop, O(n) build, no pointers and great cache behaviour. A BST gives the same O(log n) bounds plus search, predecessor/successor and delete-by-value, at the cost of pointers and constants — use it only when you need those extras (e.g. a double-ended priority queue).

How do you find the k largest elements of a stream, and why a min-heap?

Keep a min-heap of size k. For each element, push it; if the size exceeds k, pop the minimum — the smallest of the current candidates leaves. The root is always the kth largest so far. O(n log k) time and O(k) space, versus O(n log n) for sorting. A max-heap would make the largest easy to find but the one to evict hard.

Is heap sort stable? Is it used in practice?

Not stable — the long-range swaps reorder equal keys. In practice it loses to quick sort on arrays because of cache misses, but its guaranteed O(n log n) and O(1) space make it the fallback in introsort (C++ std::sort), which switches to heap sort when quick sort's recursion gets too deep.

What does decreaseKey need that a library priority queue does not provide?

The index of the element inside the heap. Library queues hide the array, so you cannot address an element. Dijkstra implementations therefore push a new (distance, vertex) pair whenever a shorter path is found and skip stale pairs when they are popped — lazy deletion — which keeps the same O(E log V) bound.
